CT417 Topic Guide

Software Architecture

Compare system-level organisation choices using the quality attributes and operational trade-offs that follow from them.

Evidence and priority

Architecture is in the current module scope, but the local papers make it a background topic rather than a recent repeating slot: it is prominent in 2019/20 but not in the 2024/25–2025/26 CI/CD/security/design-pattern sequence. Revise it, but do not give it the same prediction weight as those recent families unless current lectures emphasise it.

Rapid refresher

DistinctionExam-ready explanation
Architecture style vs design patternA style organises the whole system and its major components; a pattern is a reusable solution to a smaller recurring design problem within a context.
Monolith vs microservicesA monolith is deployed as one system; microservices deploy independently around bounded responsibilities, trading release independence for distributed-system complexity.
IaaS / PaaS / SaaSIaaS supplies infrastructure; PaaS supplies a managed application platform; SaaS supplies a finished application to users.
LayeringLayers constrain dependencies and separate concerns. An open layer may be bypassed by higher layers; a closed layer normally requires calls through adjacent layers.

How to compare architecture choices

  1. Name each style’s component/deployment organisation.
  2. Compare against the same criteria: scalability, deployment independence, fault isolation, data consistency, operational complexity and team structure.
  3. Use the scenario to justify a choice; do not present one style as universally better.

Practice question - architecture comparisons (20 marks)

Inspired by: 2019/20 Questions 1 and 4. This is a background-style question, not a claim about the current paper order.

Scenario. A university is replacing a single student-record system. It needs reliable enrolment, a mobile app, and a separate analytics team that wants to release reporting changes independently.

(a) Compare a monolithic architecture and microservices for this system. [8 marks]

Model answer: A monolith packages the enrolment, account and reporting functions into one deployable application, usually with simpler local calls, transactions, debugging and deployment. It is suitable while the system/team is small, but a reporting change still shares the release cycle and failure domain. Microservices separate responsibilities such as enrolment and reporting into independently deployable services. This can let analytics release independently and scale a busy service separately, but introduces network failure, distributed tracing, service contracts, deployment automation and cross-service data-consistency complexity. A sensible answer might retain a modular monolith initially, then split only where independent ownership/scaling justifies the operational cost.

(b) Distinguish an architectural style from a design pattern, with an example of each. [4 marks]

Model answer: Layered architecture is a system-wide style: presentation, application/service and data layers define the major organisation and allowed dependencies. Factory is a design pattern: it encapsulates object creation at a smaller code/design level. A system may use a layered style and several Factory instances; the categories operate at different scale.

(c) Distinguish IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, giving one suitable university need for each. [4 marks]

Model answer: IaaS provides virtual compute/network/storage for a team that needs control to host a custom research service. PaaS provides a managed runtime/database/deployment environment for developers who want to deploy the mobile-backend without operating servers. SaaS provides a finished application, such as hosted email or a help-desk tool, for users who only need to configure and use the service. The customer controls most on IaaS and least on SaaS.

(d) Explain the purpose of an open layer and one disadvantage. [4 marks]

Model answer: In an open layered architecture, a higher layer may call a non-adjacent lower layer directly when the intermediate layer adds no value, which can reduce overhead or expose a needed low-level capability. The disadvantage is weakened separation: clients become coupled to lower-layer details, so changes propagate more easily and testing/replacement is harder. A closed layer preserves the stricter adjacent-layer boundary.

Final check

  • Did I compare both options using matched criteria?
  • Did I tie the recommendation to the scenario rather than state a universal winner?
  • Did I keep architecture style and design pattern at their different scales?
